pulls.title: wallet: Add exportaddresskey RPC for descriptor wallets
pulls.body:
Adds `exportaddresskey "address" ( "key_type" )` to export locally available private keys for an address in a descriptor wallet. Callers can obtain private keys without identifying the descriptor index and reproducing key derivation outside Core.

The RPC has two modes:

- `wallet` (default) returns the original wallet keys, with their public keys and roles.
- `taproot_output` returns effective Taproot key-path keys using the known output commitment. Direct output keys are returned without another tweak. MuSig2 participant secrets are never combined into an aggregate private key.

Supported constructions include single-key addresses, recognized P2SH/P2WSH scripts, multisig, Miniscript, and Taproot, including MuSig2 participants. A locally available key can be exported even when the wallet cannot satisfy all spending conditions.

Lookup is limited to existing wallet metadata and known derivation indices. Encrypted wallets must be unlocked. Missing spending data, unavailable keys, and inconsistent wallet data have distinct errors.

The result contains hexadecimal private scalars, not WIF. Exported keys are not a wallet backup; scripts, cosigners, or other spending data may still be needed. Reused keys and MuSig2 participants may control other outputs.

Includes key, descriptor, wallet manager, wallet RPC, and console-history tests. Functional coverage reconstructs scripts independently and verifies spending with exported keys, partial ownership, authorization, inconsistent metadata, and absence of wallet or nonce mutation.

The initial single-key implementation was ported from [Bitcoin Roots](https://plan-b.foundation/bitcoin-roots) and now extended to cover more use-cases. Initial motivation was the lack of `dumppriv` since v30 and the need for it in the making of the [Quietproof](https://plan-b.foundation/quietproof) client.

pulls.title: rpc: fail scanblocks when block filter range is unavailable
pulls.body:
### The issue

`scanblocks` reads block filters over a range via `LookupFilterRange`. When the
block filter index is behind the active chain (e.g. right after startup, while
it is still syncing in the background), the lookup for the not yet indexed range
fails. The old code ignored that failure, advanced `start_index` to the end of
the chunk, and kept going - so the scan skipped every unindexed block and still
returned `"completed": true`.

The result is a silent gap: a caller gets a `relevant_blocks` list that looks
fine but is missing any match in the unindexed range, with no way to
distinguish "no matches" from "range was never scanned".

Note that `"completed"` only means the scan was not aborted - it does not mean
every filter in the requested range was actually read.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start a node with `-blockfilterindex=1` and let it mine/receive some blocks.
2. Stop the node, delete `<datadir>/<chain>/indexes/blockfilter`, restart with
   `-blockfilterindex=1`.
3. Immediately (before the index finishes rebuilding) call
   `scanblocks start '["addr(<addr>)"]'`.

Before this change the call returns `"completed": true` with an empty/partial
`relevant_blocks`, silently skipping the range the index had not rebuilt yet.

### How it is fixed and why

Mirror `getblockfilter`'s error classification:

- Call `BlockUntilSyncedToCurrentChain()` only to obtain an `index_ready` flag.
  Do **not** fail unconditionally when the index is still behind the tip - the
  requested range may already be available.
- If `LookupFilterRange` fails and the index is not ready, throw the same
  "still in the process of being indexed" `RPC_MISC_ERROR` that
  `getblockfilter` uses.
- If `LookupFilterRange` fails after the index is ready, throw
  `RPC_INTERNAL_ERROR` (unexpected / corruption), instead of skipping the chunk.

This closes the silent gap without rejecting scans whose range is already
covered while the index catches up to the tip.

The diff also reindents the match loop: inverting `if (LookupFilterRange(...))`
into an early `throw` removes one nesting level from the existing body. That
reindentation is a consequence of the bug fix, not a standalone style change.

### Tests

- `test/functional/rpc_scanblocks.py` - new `test_scanblocks_unindexed_range`
  covers the modified code: it pads the chain, wipes the filter index, restarts,
  and while the index is behind the tip asserts that a scan to the tip returns
  the indexing error, that a scan over an already-written prefix (genesis)
  still succeeds, and that after sync the match is found.
- The existing `run_test` cases (which `wait_until(... synced ...)` before
  scanning) continue to exercise the normal synced path.

### AI / tooling note

I found this regression while reviewing the RPC with an AI-assisted tool.
I reproduced the unsynced-index behavior myself, chose to mirror
`getblockfilter`'s existing guard, and verified the fix with the
functional test above. This PR text and any review replies are my own.

pulls.title: Test checkunparsable errors
pulls.body:
`CheckUnparsable` parses both a private-form descriptor and its corresponding public-form descriptor. The helper previously reused one error string for both parses.

The public parse therefore overwrote the private parse’s error. Although the helper verified that both parses failed, its exact error assertion only checked the error produced by the public parse. An incorrect private-form error could consequently go undetected.

## Changes

- Store the private and public parse errors separately.
- Check the exact private error when a private-form descriptor is provided.
- Continue checking the exact public error.
- Add an overload that accepts different expected private and public errors.
- Preserve the existing three-argument interface for cases where both errors should match.
- Update the affected test cases with their existing private-form errors.

This also corrects a raw descriptor test whose private input used `raw(...)` while its public input mistakenly used `sh(...)`. Both inputs now use `raw(...)`, with `Raw script is not hex` as the expected error.

This PR only changes test code and does not affect production descriptor parsing.

pulls.title: guix: compute --build triplet when lowering, not at load time
pulls.body:
### Why

`building-on` in `contrib/guix/toolchains.scm` reads `(%current-system)` once, when the module is loaded. `guix shell` loads the manifest before it applies `--system`, so the value is the system of the machine that runs the build, not the system that Guix builds for.

So a build with `ADDITIONAL_GUIX_ENVIRONMENT_FLAGS="--system=aarch64-linux"` on an x86_64 machine (for example with `qemu-binfmt-service-type`, to get an aarch64 build machine) configures the aarch64 cross toolchain with `--build=x86_64-guix-linux-gnu`. `gcc-cross-sans-libc` then fails to configure:

```
checking for CET support... configure: error: compiler and assembler with CET support are required for --enable-cet
```

### What changes

`building-on` becomes a procedure, and its three call sites call it. Guix then computes the triplet for each derivation, under the system that the derivation is built for.

### How I checked

- On master, `HOST=x86_64-linux-gnu guix shell -n --system=aarch64-linux -m contrib/guix/linux_static.scm` (with `toolchains.scm` on the load path, as `guix-build` does) gives `gcc-cross-sans-libc` with `--build=x86_64-guix-linux-gnu`. With this PR it gives `--build=aarch64-guix-linux-gnu`. That is the same derivation that `guix build -d --system=aarch64-linux` gives on master.
- Native builds (no `--system`): the toolchain derivations from `linux_static.scm` and `manifest_gui.scm` are identical on master and with this PR. So this PR does not change release builds.
- With this PR, an emulated aarch64 build of `x86_64-linux-gnu` on x86_64 built the whole cross toolchain and the non-GUI binaries. The GUI environment then failed in the tests of `python-pylint` (timeout under emulation) and `maturin` (snapshot mismatch). These packages have no aarch64 substitutes at the pinned Guix commit, and the failures are not related to this change.

pulls.title: cli: Parse -signetchallenge like bitcoind
pulls.body:
`bitcoind` returns an useful error when invalid hex is passed to `-signetchallenge`:

```
$ bitcoind -signet -signetchallenge=z
Error: -signetchallenge must be hex, not 'z'
```

The error returned by `bitcoin-cli` only indicates that the RPC cookie wasn't found. It doesn't hint at invalid hex:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -signet -signetchallenge=z getblockcount
error: Authorization failed: ...
Is your -signetchallenge correct for custom signets?
```

To have consistent validation of signet args in `bitcoind` and `bitcoin-cli`, we now parse `-signetchallenge` in a new `ReadSigNetChallengeArg()` function which is called in `ReadSigNetDir()` and `ReadSigNetArgs()`.

Addresses https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34566#discussion_r3668123074

I didn't add a release note because I don't think this change of an error message warrants one.
